question: Which competitors were mentioned, and in what context?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every mention of a competing product, vendor, or alternative solution (named or described generically, e.g. 'another automation tool', 'our current in-house scripts'), and for each state the context: who mentioned it (prospect/customer or OrbitFlow staff), what it was being compared on (features, pricing, connectors, security, ease of use, etc.), and any stated outcome or preference.
assumptions: 'Competitors' interpreted as any other vendor or alternative solution named or described in the call, including incumbent tools the customer currently uses.
No call types restricted because the question concerns all calls.
Search terms include common workflow automation competitors as examples; the reader should also capture competitors not on this list.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I'd mentally benchmarked this against Zapier, which is not a fair comparison, but that's the number that was in my head.
findings.context: Prospect benchmarked OrbitFlow pricing against Zapier, which she called an unfair comparison but the number in her head. — Pricing anchor. Rachel said Growth pricing (from $1,800/month) felt high versus Zapier.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: It's a very common anchor. It's also the wrong one, but I'd rather earn that than assert it.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff say Zapier is a common pricing anchor and the wrong comparison. — Maya's response to the Zapier pricing benchmark.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for.
findings.context: Prospect may justify OrbitFlow spend by replacing manual work and some Gainsight spend. — Cost offset. Gainsight is an existing tool the prospect pays for, not a feature comparison.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Gainsight would be useful but isn't essential.
findings.context: Gainsight would be useful for integration but is not essential. — Integration priority ranking for the pilot.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: We also have Workato. I don't want you to think we've got nothing.
findings.context: Prospect already uses Workato, which the data team uses for back-office integrations. RevOps finds it too technical, so it is not used for workflow changes. — Incumbent iPaaS. Compared on ease of use and maintainability. Tom says it works but is too technical for RevOps.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor.
findings.context: Real commercial question is whether to expand the existing Workato contract instead of adding another vendor. — Workato is the main competing alternative. Rachel says she must win this internally.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: And the honest comparison is Workato, or just improving what we already have. Not doing nothing.
findings.context: Honest comparison is Workato or improving the existing setup, not doing nothing. — Customer defines the pilot's alternatives as Workato or the status quo.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: And people compensate — they build their own reminders, their own little spreadsheets, someone wrote a script once.
findings.context: Internal in-house scripts, reminders and spreadsheets are the current workaround; prospect runs at least three scripts with unknown authors. — Build-it-yourself alternative. Compared on maintainability and ownership.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Plenty of our customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep systems integration and use us for the business-owned workflows
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff acknowledge customers keep iPaaS or internal services for deep integration and use OrbitFlow for business workflows, and that the status quo can win. — Maya frames coexistence and a no-buy outcome as valid.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: We do. It's already covered by our Microsoft agreement, which matters a lot to procurement.
findings.context: Prospect names Microsoft Power Automate as the existing automation tool the team already has, and says it is already covered by their Microsoft agreement, which matters to procurement. — Customer describing current state; compared on licensing/cost-of-procurement rather than capability.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Complex flows are difficult to monitor. And ownership becomes unclear when the creator changes role, which happens constantly.
findings.context: Prospect says Power Automate has weaknesses: complex flows are hard to monitor and ownership becomes unclear when creators change role. — Comparing Power Automate against OrbitFlow's proposed layer on maintainability and operational control.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Someone builds something in Power Automate, it works, they leave, and then it's nobody's.
findings.context: Prospect describes business teams building workflows in Power Automate that get abandoned when the creator leaves, a route-around that the backlog encourages. — Explaining why teams route around the systems group backlog.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Power Automate. Or just improving what we already have. Those are the real competitors, not another workflow vendor.
findings.context: Prospect names Power Automate and improving existing processes as the real competitors, not other workflow vendors. — Asked for the honest alternative to OrbitFlow when defining decision criteria.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Plenty of customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep integration and use us for business-owned workflows
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff say they will not replace everything and that customers often keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep integration, using OrbitFlow for business-owned workflows; prospect says a migrate-off-Microsoft proposal would lose to licensing. — Vendor positioning relative to existing Microsoft stack; prospect agrees migration proposal would fail on licensing.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Then let's define the pilot against the status quo and against Power Automate.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's account executive says a valid outcome is 'don't buy OrbitFlow' if the existing approach meets criteria more cheaply, so the pilot is defined against status quo and Power Automate. — Vendor framing of competitive evaluation.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Honestly? Zapier and Make. I like Zapier for the simple stuff, it does what it says. And I've tested Make for the more complicated branching, which it handles better than I expected.
findings.context: Customer says the real alternative to OrbitFlow is Zapier and Make; likes Zapier for simple stuff and has tested Make for more complicated branching. — Prospect's stated alternative when asked for the real alternative (not 'do nothing'); comparison on simplicity and branching capability.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Maintenance and visibility. The same two things. Make would give me the branching but I'd still have the ownership problem.
findings.context: Customer's concerns with Zapier and Make are maintenance and visibility; Make would give branching but the ownership problem remains, and only Sophie knows Make internally. — Prospect explaining downsides of the alternatives; comparison on maintenance, visibility, and internal skills.

findings.speaker: Marcus Lee
findings.quote: We've got more than sixty Zapier automations. Six-zero.
findings.context: Customer's current Zapier usage is over 60 automations, with a Zapier bill of about two hundred plus per month; the team is paying for Zapier today. — Discussion of current spend and why the comparison is about hidden costs; comparison on pricing.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership. That's a real outcome and it might be the right one.
findings.context: Prospect says budget is the biggest risk and that the team could decide it is over-buying and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership, which it views as a real outcome. — Prospect weighing OrbitFlow against keeping Zapier; comparison on price and value versus existing tool.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
findings.context: Prospect is not yet convinced the value closes the gap between OrbitFlow and the tools they already pay for. — Prospect's summary of position after demo; comparison on value versus existing tools.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: we'd have to beat Zapier plus better documentation and ownership discipline.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff frame the competition as Zapier plus better documentation and ownership discipline, and say the gain is reduced sixty independent Zaps to roughly eight reusable flows. — Vendor positioning against Zapier-based status quo; comparison on maintenance and structure.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: It's not that we do things Zapier can't. It's that sixty independent Zaps is sixty things to maintain and this is more like eight.
findings.context: Vendor claims the advantage over sixty independent Zaps is reusable subflows, so maintenance is one place to change, with about eight flows instead of sixty. — Vendor's differentiation pitch against Zapier-style independent automations; comparison on maintainability.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: We own MuleSoft, yes. And I want to be precise about this because people misunderstand it. MuleSoft is our integration backbone. It is good at that. It is not a tool that business operations should be using directly, and I would not want it to become one.
findings.context: Customer owns MuleSoft as its integration backbone and does not want to replace it; OrbitFlow positions as the business-owned layer above it, not a replacement. — Competitor/alternative is an incumbent iPaaS. Compared on role: deep system integration vs. business-operations workflows. Customer is not looking to replace it. Vendor agrees and says some customers keep an iPaaS.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: MuleSoft and custom integration services. We already own MuleSoft. If someone can demonstrate that the business-owned workflow layer can be built on top of it acceptably, that is the cheaper path even if it is the worse one.
findings.context: MuleSoft plus custom integration services is named as the cheaper alternative path to building the business-owned workflow layer. The customer thinks it is the worse option and does not think it is a good idea, but says someone will propose it. — Alternative solution compared on cost and on how workflow changes are handled. Customer says every workflow change would become an integration project, which is the problem to solve.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Some customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep systems integration and use us for business-owned workflows.
findings.context: Vendor acknowledges that some customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep systems integration and use OrbitFlow for business-owned workflows. — OrbitFlow staff describing the coexistence positioning against iPaaS/internal integration alternatives.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Replacing several departmental Python scripts with centrally visible automations and approvals.
findings.context: Departmental in-house scripts and unofficial workarounds are an existing alternative. The customer has identified 31 known scripts and plans to replace them with centrally visible automations in a later phase. — In-house scripts compared on governance, visibility and ownership. Outcome: phase two replacement use case. The count of 31 is from a non-exhaustive audit and may be incomplete.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Which are difficult for central IT to govern because central IT does not know they exist.
findings.context: Local teams build unofficial scripts to work around failed automations, and one such script ran unreviewed for four years with an over-privileged service account. — In-house scripts compared on governance and ownership. Central IT does not know they exist. The script was copying data correctly but had no owner or review.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Our people change roles constantly and individual ownership is one of the reasons our current automations decay.
findings.context: Customer's current automations decay because individual ownership changes with role changes. — Current in-house automations compared on ownership and maintainability. Customer wants team-owned exception queues.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: We have bought software before that demonstrated beautifully and then could not reach our systems.
findings.context: Customer previously bought software that demonstrated well but could not reach their systems. Vendor name not given. — Previous unnamed software vendors compared on deployment architecture and connectivity to internal systems. Customer prioritises architecture over demos for this reason.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: I spoke to a workflow vendor there and I cannot remember which one, and it has been irritating me for two months.
findings.context: Another unnamed workflow vendor was met at Hannover Messe in April. The customer cannot remember which one. — Unnamed competitor mentioned off-topic. No comparison or outcome stated. OrbitFlow staff did not identify the vendor and asked to hear it later.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: That is an honest answer. Most vendors say "yes, it handles that."
findings.context: Other vendors generically claim they handle contract amendments mid-run; the customer found OrbitFlow's more explicit answer more honest. — Competitor claims compared on handling of mid-workflow state changes (contract amendments). Customer's view is that OrbitFlow's answer stood out from typical vendor responses.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: If you do that, you will be the second vendor this year who has.
findings.context: A previous vendor provided a transparent pricing breakdown; the customer says OrbitFlow would be the second vendor that year to do so. First vendor not named. — Competitor compared on pricing transparency and professional services disclosure. Customer says the first vendor is not something they will name.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: You and Tray.io. We've had a Tray proof of concept running for about six weeks.
findings.context: Ember Financial is running a bake-off between OrbitFlow and Tray.io, with a Tray.io proof of concept already running for about six weeks. — Customer frames the evaluation; Tray is the named competitor in the bake-off.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Connector breadth is genuinely good. No complaints there.
findings.context: Tray.io's connector breadth is good; the customer's main criticism of Tray is the debugging experience on large visual workflows. — Comparison on connectors and debugging/ease of use with the Tray PoC.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: When something goes wrong at step forty of a sixty-step flow, the debugging experience is — it's not good.
findings.context: Engineers find debugging large visual workflows in Tray hard; a failure at step forty of a sixty-step flow is hard to diagnose. — Criticism of Tray on debugging experience.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Retry semantics were opaque. We couldn't always tell whether something had run twice.
findings.context: Tray's retry semantics were opaque in the PoC, and the team could not always tell whether something had run twice. — Comparison on error handling and idempotency with the Tray PoC.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
findings.context: Debugging experience and programmatic audit export are the deciding factors for choosing OrbitFlow over Tray; connector breadth is a tie. — Customer states what must be true to choose OrbitFlow over Tray.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: It's also "keep the scripts and document them better." That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
findings.context: The main alternative is keeping the existing scripts and documenting them better; it is cheaper and likely to be proposed internally, but would not satisfy the auditor. — Customer describes an in-house alternative as the honest comparison; compared on cost and auditability.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: It wouldn't satisfy the auditor. But it would be proposed, and somebody senior would find it attractive, and we'd spend two months on it.
findings.context: Documenting the scripts would not satisfy the auditor, but it could still be proposed and absorb about two months. — Hannah's view on the in-house scripts alternative.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Then let's address it in the pilot criteria explicitly rather than pretending the only alternative is Tray.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff framed the in-house scripts/Slack alternative as a choice to address explicitly in pilot criteria rather than pretending Tray is the only alternative. — OrbitFlow response to the in-house alternative; vendor reasoning on competitive framing.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: It's searchable. It's not auditable.
findings.context: Current exception handling runs on Slack channels and custom scripts, which the customer describes as searchable but not auditable. — Incumbent in-house process, not a vendor; the auditor found it not evidenced.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I wouldn't say it's a toy, it does about eighty percent of what we need.
findings.context: Prospect pushes back on the vendor's 'toy' characterization of Zapier, saying it covers about 80% of their needs. — Customer contradicts vendor's dismissal of Zapier; shows Zapier is judged adequate by the prospect.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: he'll ask what we get for twenty-one thousand that we don't get from Zapier for two thousand, and I need a better answer than "it's more robust."
findings.context: Prospect questions what OrbitFlow's roughly £21k annual price buys versus Zapier at about £2k. — Price comparison against Zapier; prospect's founder would need a better answer than 'it's more robust' to approve.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough for a company that doesn't have an IT team. That's a real possibility
findings.context: Prospect says they may stay with Zapier plus better process discipline rather than buy OrbitFlow, a real alternative under consideration. — Status-quo alternative raised on price and complexity; prospect says it is a real possibility, though undecided.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: Two other vendors we've spoken to had it as an enterprise-only feature and I'd be surprised if you were different.
findings.context: Prospect has spoken to two other unnamed vendors that treat SSO as an enterprise-only feature, which contrasts with OrbitFlow's claim it is included on all plans. — Competitor comparison on security/SSO packaging; the competing vendors are not named.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: We use it heavily. And we get favourable licensing on it, which matters more than I'd like it to.
findings.context: Power Automate is the incumbent automation tool at Greenline, used heavily, and is favourably licensed. — Customer describes the incumbent; comparison framed around licensing cost and embedded use. Customer says favourable licensing matters more than they'd like.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it. For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
findings.context: Power Automate is embedded, licensed, approved, and liked by the platform team, making it the decisive competitive gap versus OrbitFlow on Dynamics integration. — Customer compares OrbitFlow against Power Automate on first-class Dynamics connectivity and organisational fit; OrbitFlow staff acknowledged the gap.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: But complex flows are hard for operations to troubleshoot. When something breaks, it comes to my team, and my team is six people supporting two and a half thousand.
findings.context: Power Automate's flows are hard for operations to troubleshoot, which is a pain point OrbitFlow could address. — Customer's criticism of the incumbent on troubleshooting and support burden, which is the basis for the operational-cost argument against it.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: If the decision is purely cost per seat, Microsoft wins and everyone knows it. The argument has to be that the operational cost
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff acknowledged Power Automate has bundled licensing that OrbitFlow cannot beat on price; the argument must be operational cost instead. — OrbitFlow concedes on licence cost versus Microsoft bundling and reframes the comparison around support cost.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Do the same test in Power Automate at the same time. If it's not better, you should know.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff suggested benchmarking OrbitFlow against Power Automate on the same reusability and debugging test. — Comparison on reusability and ease of debugging; OrbitFlow proposes a head-to-head test and expects it may not favour them.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The Microsoft platform team will not want this. Not because it's bad. Because it isn't Microsoft.
findings.context: The Microsoft platform team is expected to strongly oppose OrbitFlow because it is not Microsoft, and has killed things before. — Internal stakeholder preference for Microsoft-native tooling; this is a competitive-alternative preference rather than a feature comparison.

findings.speaker: Lucy Hart
findings.quote: two of them already have local Power Automate specialists. So the operating model isn't completely centralised today
findings.context: Customer team builds its own automations in-house in two regions (North and South West) using local Power Automate specialists, which is an existing alternative to a central solution. — Correction to Carlos's earlier claim; regional in-house building is a current alternative approach.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: You've got Power Automate.
findings.context: Customer names Microsoft Power Automate as the incumbent tool used for low-risk administrative tasks, and says it works for that. — Incumbent competitor; customer compares it on fit for low-risk admin tasks. Customer says it works for that use but lacks monitoring and reusable components.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: It's used for low-risk administrative tasks — document routing, some notifications. It works for that.
findings.context: Power Automate is used for low-risk administrative tasks such as document routing and some notifications, and works for that. — Incumbent comparison; customer says it works within its scope.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: Monitoring, mostly. And reusable components. The transformation team wants better monitoring and reusable components
findings.context: Customer says the incumbent lacks monitoring and reusable components, which the transformation team wants. — Gaps in the Power Automate incumbent; customer's stated reason for wanting change.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: There's also internal development. We build things. That's the other alternative and it's the one that appeals to certain people.
findings.context: Internal development by the firm's own small team is an alternative to buying a platform; customer says it appeals to some people and is argued as understanding their systems better than a vendor. — Build-in-house alternative; compared on ownership and capacity. Customer notes the team is already at capacity and would own it forever.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: we understand our own systems better than a vendor does.
findings.context: Internal development argument: the firm's team understands its own systems better than a vendor; counter-argument is ownership forever and team already at capacity. — Internal build option; customer describes both sides of the decision.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: It's usually decided by whoever has the loudest voice rather than by a cost comparison.
findings.context: Vendor says the internal-build vs. vendor decision is usually decided by loudest voice rather than cost comparison. — OrbitFlow staff comment on the build-versus-buy decision in general, not a product comparison.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: Customer success uses a limited Gainsight deployment. Limited meaning we bought it, we implemented about forty percent of it, and then the person who owned it left.
findings.context: Customer success uses a limited Gainsight deployment; OrbitFlow's proposed alternative is expanding Gainsight, which the customer frames as the competing option. — Gainsight is the incumbent CS tool at Inkwell. Only about 40% was implemented after the owner left; the customer attributes that to implementation failure, not licensing. Expansion of Gainsight is described as the alternative someone will propose.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Gainsight has the customer success concepts but we haven't implemented them.
findings.context: Gainsight has customer success concepts but was not implemented; the customer says it does not provide the cross-system workflow. — Compared on cross-system workflow capability. Darren Wu says Gainsight lacks the workflow, and that nothing joins Zendesk, Snowflake, and Salesforce into an action.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: It's the alternative I'd propose if the cost comparison favoured it.
findings.context: Expanding Gainsight is a real alternative the customer may favour if the cost comparison supports it; OrbitFlow agreed to build an honest comparison including it. — Cost comparison requested by customer including implementation effort on both sides. Maya Chen says she will build the comparison including Gainsight and says she would rather lose if Gainsight is cheaper.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: And a chunk of what we're notionally paying Gainsight for.
findings.context: The Gainsight spend is questioned by the customer, and a cost model comparing OrbitFlow with expanding Gainsight will surface it. — Pricing context. Olivia Grant says a chunk of Gainsight spend is questionable and could be consolidated. Darren Wu disagrees that Gainsight will be switched off. Maya Chen notes the comparison will surface the spend.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: And my team has built a set of Looker alerts. Which work, but they're alerts. They tell you something and then nothing happens.
findings.context: Inkwell's Looker alerts are an internal, in-house alternative that surfaces data but cannot trigger action. — Current tooling compared on ability to produce action. Darren Wu says the alerts work but have no follow-through.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Looker has the data but no ability to make anything happen.
findings.context: Looker has the data but no ability to make anything happen. — Compared on workflow/action capability versus OrbitFlow's proposed workflow.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: that's a problem you'd have with any approach, including buying Gainsight properly. It's not an OrbitFlow problem.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff say the Gainsight comparison problem (lacking outcome data on fine accounts) applies to any approach, including buying Gainsight properly, so it is not an OrbitFlow-specific problem. — OrbitFlow's view on measurement limits, framed as applying to Gainsight too.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: Or we've looked at Retool Workflows, which is honestly quite close to what you do.
findings.context: Prospect's engineering lead named Retool Workflows as a build-alternative that is 'quite close' to OrbitFlow, and the team has looked at it. — Customer (Ava Sinclair) raising an alternative to buying OrbitFlow, compared on overall capability; OrbitFlow staff acknowledged the comparison without disparaging it.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Retool Workflows is a reasonable comparison and I'm not going to pretend it isn't.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's Solutions Engineer conceded Retool Workflows is a reasonable comparison. — OrbitFlow staff response to the Retool mention; no outcome or preference stated.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: Step Functions, probably.
findings.context: The main alternative under consideration is building internally on AWS Step Functions. — Customer's build-vs-buy alternative; compared on build effort and ownership cost. Prospect's VP argues against it on maintenance grounds, favouring buying.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: I think most of what you do could be built internally. We have the skills. The question is whether we should.
findings.context: Internal build (in-house) is the main alternative; prospect's VP argues owning it long-term is the real cost and that the engineer would be overloaded. — Customer VP favours OrbitFlow on maintenance grounds; the engineer believes most of it could be built internally.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: That's what happened with our observability vendor.
findings.context: Prospect's prior observability vendor drove cost problems via per-event pricing, which the prospect cites as a reason to avoid per-event billing. — Customer mention of a past competing vendor, compared on pricing model; outcome was a bad experience ('twice').

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: At my last company I pushed through a tool over engineering's objection and it was a disaster for eighteen months.
findings.context: Prospect's VP says a previous tool he pushed through over engineering's objection was a disaster for eighteen months (at a former company). — Former-employer tool, not the same as a current evaluation competitor; mentioned as background on sponsor's risk.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: We lose deals that way. We lose fewer customers.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff said they lose deals to competitors over undertested or overpromised claims, and lose fewer customers that way. — Vendor commentary on evaluation rigor; no named competitor.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: We came from that. That was the Zapier estate.
findings.context: Customer says Lumen came from Zapier; the prior Zapier estate was the tool they moved off of. — Mentioned as a previous platform, not a live competitor in this renewal. Raised in the context of governance and clutter, not features, pricing, or connectors. No comparison or stated preference between Zapier and OrbitFlow.

findings.speaker: Devan Shah
findings.quote: Sixty-odd Zaps, half of them orphaned.
findings.context: Devan Shah describes the legacy Zapier estate as sixty-odd Zaps, half of them orphaned. — Describes the prior Zapier setup as a governance problem (orphaned automations), which he links to the current OrbitFlow naming and cleanup discussion. No stated preference on features or pricing.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: I had a depot manager tell me in July that he'd stopped keeping his own spreadsheet
findings.context: Before OrbitFlow, a depot manager kept his own spreadsheet to track exceptions; he has since stopped. — Manual spreadsheet tracking is an alternative solution the customer used. Fiona presents its abandonment as evidence of OrbitFlow's value in depot exception handling. Comparison is implicit, not on features or price.

findings.speaker: Fiona Bright
findings.quote: Everything else we could go back to doing the old way and survive.
findings.context: Without OrbitFlow, Lumen could go back to the old manual way of working for most processes, but depot exception routing would be painful to lose. — Fiona names the status quo / manual process as the fallback. She says it is survivable for everything except depot exception routing, which she would miss most. This is a stated alternative, with the preference favouring OrbitFlow for that workflow.

findings.speaker: Nadia Rahman
findings.quote: She wants it in Guidewire.
findings.context: Customer's claims director prefers moving claims triage into Guidewire rather than keeping it in OrbitFlow, and the customer sees her point because claims handlers already work in Guidewire. — Guidewire is an alternative home for the claims triage workflows that were the original reason for buying OrbitFlow. The director changed in April, and the customer says she has a different view on where triage should happen. Stated as a preference, not a decision.

findings.speaker: Nadia Rahman
findings.quote: Not natively. That's what we'd have to build.
findings.context: Customer says Guidewire cannot natively do the cross-system part of claims triage (pulling from the broker portal and document store), so that would have to be built. — Compared on cross-system integration capability. Guidewire is the alternative for claims triage. The customer's answer to the vendor's question was that it would have to be built with another tool.

findings.speaker: Nadia Rahman
findings.quote: Power Automate, probably.
findings.context: Customer names Microsoft Power Automate as the likely tool for building the cross-system part of claims triage if it moves to Guidewire. — Power Automate is a possible alternative for the cross-system build, offered alongside Guidewire's own integration layer. The customer said 'probably', so this is not a firm choice.

findings.speaker: Nadia Rahman
findings.quote: Guidewire's own integration layer, which our vendor tells us is capable and our developers tell me is painful.
findings.context: Guidewire's own integration layer is an alternative for the cross-system work. evidence.context: Tray.io's connector breadth is good; the customer's main criticism of Tray is the debugging experience on large visual workflows. — Comparison on connectors and debugging/ease of use with the Tray PoC.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: When something goes wrong at step forty of a sixty-step flow, the debugging experience is — it's not good.
evidence.context: Engineers find debugging large visual workflows in Tray hard; a failure at step forty of a sixty-step flow is hard to diagnose. — Criticism of Tray on debugging experience.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Retry semantics were opaque. We couldn't always tell whether something had run twice.
evidence.context: Tray's retry semantics were opaque in the PoC, and the team could not always tell whether something had run twice. — Comparison on error handling and idempotency with the Tray PoC.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
evidence.context: Debugging experience and programmatic audit export are the deciding factors for choosing OrbitFlow over Tray; connector breadth is a tie. — Customer states what must be true to choose OrbitFlow over Tray.

evidence.speaker: Rafael Santos
evidence.quote: We're three weeks into evaluating Tray.io.
evidence.context: Prospect is evaluating Tray.io as a competing vendor and is three weeks into the evaluation with a decision coming mid-October. — Customer-side mention of a named competitor; the evaluation is the main competitive context. Decision date is mid-October (around the 14th).

evidence.speaker: Rafael Santos
evidence.quote: Well. Genuinely well. Their team's been good.
evidence.context: Prospect says Tray's team has been good and the evaluation is going well. — Customer's view of Tray during the evaluation; no performance problems stated at this point.

evidence.speaker: Rafael Santos
evidence.quote: Tray don't have a connector and we're looking at building against its API
evidence.context: Tray.io has no connector for the prospect's mid-market manufacturing ERP, so building against its API is being considered; the prospect's developer estimates three weeks, which the prospect thinks will be six. — Comparison on connectors/integration with the prospect's ERP. This is the one area the prospect says is not going well in the Tray evaluation.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: It isn't. We lose to them and we beat them and it usually comes down to fit rather than quality.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff says Tray is not bad, that OrbitFlow both loses to and beats Tray, and that outcomes usually come down to fit rather than quality. — OrbitFlow's characterization of a named competitor; vendor-side, not customer-side.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: we probably don't have a native connector, and you'd be building against the API with our generic REST action.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff says they probably have no native connector for the prospect's ERP either, offering a generic REST action that would take the same time, so no advantage on that point. — Vendor concedes no connector advantage versus Tray on the ERP integration; compared on connectors. Vendor claims a possible advantage only on maintainability and reuse, which it calls subtler.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Run it against Tray — I mean that, run it against Tray
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff suggests the prospect run a one-week test where operations staff build a workflow without the developer, and to run it against Tray; if Tray passes, buy Tray. — Vendor recommends a competitor-neutral evaluation test that includes the named competitor, comparing on ease of process change by non-developers.

claims.text: Gainsight is an incumbent at Acme (possible spend offset) and Inkwell Learning (about 40% implemented). Inkwell's Darren Wu would propose expanding it if the cost comparison favoured it, and Maya Chen agreed to build that comparison. Looker alerts at Inkwell show data but trigger no action.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for.
evidence.context: Prospect may justify OrbitFlow spend by replacing manual work and some Gainsight spend. — Cost offset. Gainsight is an existing tool the prospect pays for, not a feature comparison.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Gainsight would be useful but isn't essential.
evidence.context: Gainsight would be useful for integration but is not essential. — Integration priority ranking for the pilot.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: Customer success uses a limited Gainsight deployment. Limited meaning we bought it, we implemented about forty percent of it, and then the person who owned it left.
evidence.context: Customer success uses a limited Gainsight deployment; OrbitFlow's proposed alternative is expanding Gainsight, which the customer frames as the competing option. — Gainsight is the incumbent CS tool at Inkwell. Only about 40% was implemented after the owner left; the customer attributes that to implementation failure, not licensing. Expansion of Gainsight is described as the alternative someone will propose.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: Gainsight has the customer success concepts but we haven't implemented them.
evidence.context: Gainsight has customer success concepts but was not implemented; the customer says it does not provide the cross-system workflow. — Compared on cross-system workflow capability. Darren Wu says Gainsight lacks the workflow, and that nothing joins Zendesk, Snowflake, and Salesforce into an action.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: It's the alternative I'd propose if the cost comparison favoured it.
evidence.context: Expanding Gainsight is a real alternative the customer may favour if the cost comparison supports it; OrbitFlow agreed to build an honest comparison including it. — Cost comparison requested by customer including implementation effort on both sides. Maya Chen says she will build the comparison including Gainsight and says she would rather lose if Gainsight is cheaper.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: And a chunk of what we're notionally paying Gainsight for.
evidence.context: The Gainsight spend is questioned by the customer, and a cost model comparing OrbitFlow with expanding Gainsight will surface it. — Pricing context. Olivia Grant says a chunk of Gainsight spend is questionable and could be consolidated. Darren Wu disagrees that Gainsight will be switched off. Maya Chen notes the comparison will surface the spend.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: that's a problem you'd have with any approach, including buying Gainsight properly. It's not an OrbitFlow problem.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff say the Gainsight comparison problem (lacking outcome data on fine accounts) applies to any approach, including buying Gainsight properly, so it is not an OrbitFlow-specific problem. — OrbitFlow's view on measurement limits, framed as applying to Gainsight too.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: And my team has built a set of Looker alerts. Which work, but they're alerts. They tell you something and then nothing happens.
evidence.context: Inkwell's Looker alerts are an internal, in-house alternative that surfaces data but cannot trigger action. — Current tooling compared on ability to produce action. Darren Wu says the alerts work but have no follow-through.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: Looker has the data but no ability to make anything happen.
evidence.context: Looker has the data but no ability to make anything happen. — Compared on workflow/action capability versus OrbitFlow's proposed workflow.

claims.text: Other named alternatives: DeltaWorks owns MuleSoft as its integration backbone and does not want to replace it, though MuleSoft plus custom services is the cheaper path someone may propose. Juniper Cloud Tools cites Retool Workflows (a reasonable comparison, per Nina Patel) and AWS Step Functions. evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: We own MuleSoft, yes. And I want to be precise about this because people misunderstand it. MuleSoft is our integration backbone. It is good at that. It is not a tool that business operations should be using directly, and I would not want it to become one.
evidence.context: Customer owns MuleSoft as its integration backbone and does not want to replace it; OrbitFlow positions as the business-owned layer above it, not a replacement. — Competitor/alternative is an incumbent iPaaS. Compared on role: deep system integration vs. business-operations workflows. Customer is not looking to replace it. Vendor agrees and says some customers keep an iPaaS.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: MuleSoft and custom integration services. We already own MuleSoft. If someone can demonstrate that the business-owned workflow layer can be built on top of it acceptably, that is the cheaper path even if it is the worse one.
evidence.context: MuleSoft plus custom integration services is named as the cheaper alternative path to building the business-owned workflow layer. The customer thinks it is the worse option and does not think it is a good idea, but says someone will propose it. — Alternative solution compared on cost and on how workflow changes are handled. Customer says every workflow change would become an integration project, which is the problem to solve.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Some customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep systems integration and use us for business-owned workflows.
evidence.context: Vendor acknowledges that some customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep systems integration and use OrbitFlow for business-owned workflows. — OrbitFlow staff describing the coexistence positioning against iPaaS/internal integration alternatives.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: Or we've looked at Retool Workflows, which is honestly quite close to what you do.
evidence.context: Prospect's engineering lead named Retool Workflows as a build-alternative that is 'quite close' to OrbitFlow, and the team has looked at it. — Customer (Ava Sinclair) raising an alternative to buying OrbitFlow, compared on overall capability; OrbitFlow staff acknowledged the comparison without disparaging it.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: Retool Workflows is a reasonable comparison and I'm not going to pretend it isn't.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow's Solutions Engineer conceded Retool Workflows is a reasonable comparison. — OrbitFlow staff response to the Retool mention; no outcome or preference stated.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: Step Functions, probably.
evidence.context: The main alternative under consideration is building internally on AWS Step Functions. — Customer's build-vs-buy alternative; compared on build effort and ownership cost. Prospect's VP argues against it on maintenance grounds, favouring buying.

evidence.speaker: Nadia Rahman
evidence.quote: She wants it in Guidewire.
evidence.context: Customer's claims director prefers moving claims triage into Guidewire rather than keeping it in OrbitFlow, and the customer sees her point because claims handlers already work in Guidewire. — Guidewire is an alternative home for the claims triage workflows that were the original reason for buying OrbitFlow. The director changed in April, and the customer says she has a different view on where triage should happen. Stated as a preference, not a decision.

evidence.speaker: Nadia Rahman
evidence.quote: Not natively. That's what we'd have to build.
evidence.context: Customer says Guidewire cannot natively do the cross-system part of claims triage (pulling from the broker portal and document store), so that would have to be built. — Compared on cross-system integration capability. Guidewire is the alternative for claims triage. The customer's answer to the vendor's question was that it would have to be built with another tool.

evidence.speaker: Nadia Rahman
evidence.quote: Guidewire's own integration layer, which our vendor tells us is capable and our developers tell me is painful.
evidence.context: Guidewire's own integration layer is an alternative for the cross-system work. The vendor says it is capable, but the customer's developers say it is painful. — Compared on ease of use and capability. The customer reports a conflict between the Guidewire vendor's claims and the developers' experience, and says they trust the developers.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: if the Guidewire route works out you were right.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow's account lead acknowledges that moving to Guidewire could be the right outcome, and that if it works, the customer was right not to renew. — OrbitFlow staff framing of the Guidewire route as a legitimate alternative to renewing. This is the vendor's own view, not a customer statement.

claims.text: In-house scripts, spreadsheets and internal builds were repeatedly named as the alternative, at Acme, DeltaWorks, Ember Financial, Harbor Legal, Juniper, Verity and Lumen. Several vendors framed 'don't buy' or the status quo as a valid outcome.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: And people compensate — they build their own reminders, their own little spreadsheets, someone wrote a script once.
evidence.context: Internal in-house scripts, reminders and spreadsheets are the current workaround; prospect runs at least three scripts with unknown authors. — Build-it-yourself alternative. Compared on maintainability and ownership.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Plenty of our customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep systems integration and use us for the business-owned workflows
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff acknowledge customers keep iPaaS or internal services for deep integration and use OrbitFlow for business workflows, and that the status quo can win. — Maya frames coexistence and a no-buy outcome as valid.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Replacing several departmental Python scripts with centrally visible automations and approvals.
evidence.context: Departmental in-house scripts and unofficial workarounds are an existing alternative. The customer has identified 31 known scripts and plans to replace them with centrally visible automations in a later phase. — In-house scripts compared on governance, visibility and ownership. Outcome: phase two replacement use case. The count of 31 is from a non-exhaustive audit and may be incomplete.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Which are difficult for central IT to govern because central IT does not know they exist.
evidence.context: Local teams build unofficial scripts to work around failed automations, and one such script ran unreviewed for four years with an over-privileged service account. — In-house scripts compared on governance and ownership. Central IT does not know they exist. The script was copying data correctly but had no owner or review.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: It's also "keep the scripts and document them better." That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
evidence.context: The main alternative is keeping the existing scripts and documenting them better; it is cheaper and likely to be proposed internally, but would not satisfy the auditor. — Customer describes an in-house alternative as the honest comparison; compared on cost and auditability.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: It wouldn't satisfy the auditor. But it would be proposed, and somebody senior would find it attractive, and we'd spend two months on it.
evidence.context: Documenting the scripts would not satisfy the auditor, but it could still be proposed and absorb about two months. — Hannah's view on the in-house scripts alternative.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Then let's address it in the pilot criteria explicitly rather than pretending the only alternative is Tray.
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff framed the in-house scripts/Slack alternative as a choice to address explicitly in pilot criteria rather than pretending Tray is the only alternative. — OrbitFlow response to the in-house alternative; vendor reasoning on competitive framing.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: There's also internal development. We build things. That's the other alternative and it's the one that appeals to certain people.
evidence.context: Internal development by the firm's own small team is an alternative to buying a platform; customer says it appeals to some people and is argued as understanding their systems better than a vendor. — Build-in-house alternative; compared on ownership and capacity. Customer notes the team is already at capacity and would own it forever.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: we understand our own systems better than a vendor does.
evidence.context: Internal development argument: the firm's team understands its own systems better than a vendor; counter-argument is ownership forever and team already at capacity. — Internal build option; customer describes both sides of the decision.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: It's usually decided by whoever has the loudest voice rather than by a cost comparison.
evidence.context: Vendor says the internal-build vs. vendor decision is usually decided by loudest voice rather than cost comparison. — OrbitFlow staff comment on the build-versus-buy decision in general, not a product comparison.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: I think most of what you do could be built internally. We have the skills. The question is whether we should.
evidence.context: Internal build (in-house) is the main alternative; prospect's VP argues owning it long-term is the real cost and that the engineer would be overloaded. — Customer VP favours OrbitFlow on maintenance grounds; the engineer believes most of it could be built internally.

evidence.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
evidence.quote: two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.
evidence.context: An in-house build was an alternative Verity's engineers pushed for for about eighteen months before the customer ran out of arguments against it. — Build-in-house alternative; the stated reason for leaving was maintenance, which the customer argued would also apply to the platform.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: I had a depot manager tell me in July that he'd stopped keeping his own spreadsheet
evidence.context: Before OrbitFlow, a depot manager kept his own spreadsheet to track exceptions; he has since stopped. — Manual spreadsheet tracking is an alternative solution the customer used. Fiona presents its abandonment as evidence of OrbitFlow's value in depot exception handling. Comparison is implicit, not on features or price.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Everything else we could go back to doing the old way and survive.
evidence.context: Without OrbitFlow, Lumen could go back to the old manual way of working for most processes, but depot exception routing would be painful to lose. — Fiona names the status quo / manual process as the fallback. She says it is survivable for everything except depot exception routing, which she would miss most. This is a stated alternative, with the preference favouring OrbitFlow for that workflow.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Plenty of customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep integration and use us for business-owned workflows
evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff say they will not replace everything and that customers often keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep integration, using OrbitFlow for business-owned workflows; prospect says a migrate-off-Microsoft proposal would lose to licensing. — Vendor positioning relative to existing Microsoft stack; prospect agrees migration proposal would fail on licensing.

claims.text: Unnamed vendors: DeltaWorks met an unremembered workflow vendor at Hannover Messe and had a prior vendor with transparent pricing. Fable Media spoke to two vendors that gate SSO as enterprise-only. Juniper's prior observability vendor used per-event pricing.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: I spoke to a workflow vendor there and I cannot remember which one, and it has been irritating me for two months.
evidence.context: Another unnamed workflow vendor was met at Hannover Messe in April. The customer cannot remember which one. — Unnamed competitor mentioned off-topic. No comparison or outcome stated. OrbitFlow staff did not identify the vendor and asked to hear it later.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: That is an honest answer. Most vendors say "yes, it handles that."
evidence.context: Other vendors generically claim they handle contract amendments mid-run; the customer found OrbitFlow's more explicit answer more honest. — Competitor claims compared on handling of mid-workflow state changes (contract amendments). Customer's view is that OrbitFlow's answer stood out from typical vendor responses.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: If you do that, you will be the second vendor this year who has.
evidence.context: A previous vendor provided a transparent pricing breakdown; the customer says OrbitFlow would be the second vendor that year to do so. First vendor not named. — Competitor compared on pricing transparency and professional services disclosure. Customer says the first vendor is not something they will name.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: We have bought software before that demonstrated beautifully and then could not reach our systems.
evidence.context: Customer previously bought software that demonstrated well but could not reach their systems. Vendor name not given. — Previous unnamed software vendors compared on deployment architecture and connectivity to internal systems. Customer prioritises architecture over demos for this reason.

evidence.speaker: Ben Foster
evidence.quote: Two other vendors we've spoken to had it as an enterprise-only feature and I'd be surprised if you were different.
evidence.context: Prospect has spoken to two other unnamed vendors that treat SSO as an enterprise-only feature, which contrasts with OrbitFlow's claim it is included on all plans. — Competitor comparison on security/SSO packaging; the competing vendors are not named.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: That's what happened with our observability vendor.
evidence.context: Prospect's prior observability vendor drove cost problems via per-event pricing, which the prospect cites as a reason to avoid per-event billing. — Customer mention of a past competing vendor, compared on pricing model; outcome was a bad experience ('twice').
